newsitem.title: USA: Couple to plead guilty in taped Gingrich phone call.
newsitem.headline: Couple to plead guilty in taped Gingrich phone call.

text.p: A Florida couple has agreed to plead guilty to illegally intercepting a phone call between House Speaker Newt Gingrich and his top lieutenants in December, the Justice Department said Wednesday.

It said John and Alice Martin each were charged with one count of using a radio scanner to intentionally intercept the cellular telephone call on Dec. 21, 1996. They also signed agreements to enter a guilty plea.
They were charged with the lowest level of offence, "an infraction," which carries a maximum $5,000 fine. It does not provide for any time in prison.
The charges and the plea agreements were filed in federal court in Jacksonville, Fla., and announced by the Justice Department in Washington, D.C.

The Martins told a news conference in January that they were monitoring the cellular phone conversation on a police scanner while driving near Jacksonville. When they recognised the voices they taped the conversation.

They said they gave the tape to Representative Karen Thurman, Democrat of Florida, and then passed it to the House ethics committee's top Democrat, Representative Jim McDermott of Washington, on Thurman's advice while visiting Congress.
The New York Times then published excerpts of the conference call among Gingrich, other House Republicans and aides discussing the ethics case against the speaker.
On the day of the phone call, Gingrich had agreed to concede to ethics committee findings that he had committed violations of ethics rules.
As part of the plea agreement, the Martins agreed to provide "truthful and candid" cooperation regarding the incident.

U.S. Attorney Charles Wilson said, "The Martins were charged with the most serious violation possible based on the applicable federal law and the circumstances surrounding the interception of the telephone call."

Scot Charney of the Justice Department's computer crime section, said, "All Americans are entitled to privacy in their telephone communications. Americans should know that intentionally intercepting other peoples' calls is illegal."
